input.rationale: Interpret the VerifyLeader execution: with the leader cut from both other voters and the two non-voters reachable, verification succeeded against a voter quorum of two; with the non-voters also cut it failed and the leader stepped down. The question is recorded as violated with the supporter-set defect asserted, and the lease-bounded window, absent client reads and partition modelling are kept as counterevidence and limits.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. VerifyLeader reports success although the leader can reach fewer voters than the voter quorum it sized, because acknowledgements arriving on non-voter replication streams are counted as support. Evidence from receipt 7a54f3754b0b423aaf1ba6c0365367c0 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0). Parsed index 1, the trigger: five members were bootstrapped, two were demoted to non-voters, and the leader's transport was disconnected in both directions from the two remaining voters, so voters_reachable=1 against quorum_voters=2 while nonvoters_reachable=2; VerifyLeader completed with verify_ok=true and an empty error, and the node was still Leader. Parsed index 3, the control on an identically built cluster with the non-voters also disconnected (nonvoters_reachable=0): the same call completed with verify_ok=false and the error 'leadership lost while committing log', the node by then a Follower. The two cases differ only in whether the non-voters could answer, so the successful verification in the trigger is attributable to non-voter acknowledgements rather than to voter support. Mechanism from source: verifyLeader sets quorumSize with quorumSize(), which counts only voters (raft.go:1087-1100), but registers the verify future on every entry of leaderState.replState (raft.go:966-990), and startStopReplication creates a replication state for every configured server including non-voters (raft.go:583-600); any successful heartbeat or AppendEntries response calls notifyAll(true) (replication.go:100-112), which increments the verify future's vote count (future.go:274-293) and completes it at the voter-sized quorum. The library already uses the correct supporter set one function away: checkLeaderLease iterates the latest configuration and counts only voters (raft.go:1037-1050), so the two paths disagree about who can establish leadership. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a client that calls VerifyLeader to protect a read (api.go:927-931) is told the leader still holds a voter quorum while it can reach none of the other voters, so the guard against serving stale reads after leadership loss does not hold in a cluster that contains non-voters.

knowledge.assertion: VerifyLeader sizes a voter quorum but registers the verification on every replication stream, including non-voters, whose acks increment its vote count.
checkLeaderLease counts only voters, unlike VerifyLeader.

counterevidence: The verification returned before the lease check stepped the leader down, so the false success is bounded by the leader lease interval rather than permanent; in the control that same step-down produced the error the trigger avoided.
VerifyLeader returning nil installed no leader and returned no data; the harm requires a client to rely on it as the guard the documentation describes, and this harness issued no reads.

Non-voter reachability does show the leader is alive and connected, so a deployment that used VerifyLeader only as a liveness probe would not be affected; the code sizes a voter quorum, which makes quorum the stated intent.
The partition was modelled by removing in-memory transport routing in both directions between the leader and the voters, not by dropping packets or crashing members.
limitations: One configuration shape was exercised: three voters and two non-voters, with the leader cut from both other voters. Other suffrage mixes, a single non-voter, or a non-voter whose heartbeat is the only one in flight were not tested.

The exposure window was not measured directly: the harness observed the verification completing immediately after the partition and the leader still in Leader state; how long a false success could persist before the lease check stepped the leader down is bounded by LeaderLeaseTimeout (one second here) but was not sampled.
No client reads were issued, so the end-to-end stale-read consequence is inferred from the documented purpose of VerifyLeader rather than observed.
The demotions completed before the partition, but each member's view of the new configuration was not read back before the transport was cut.

Parsed index 3 (control, retained state of a real single-node cluster that committed 8300 commands through the leader/commit/apply path, restarted with a snapshot at index 8302 at or above the staged commit index 8301, replay 0 batches) recorded returned=true in 0 ms. Parsed index 5 (seeded store, 8193 committed entries = 129 batches, one entry past the channel capacity) recorded returned=false after 5000 ms with exactly one newly blocked goroutine matching (*Raft).processLogs and one matching (*Raft).restoreFromCommittedLogs. interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A leadership transfer that explicitly names a member the committed configuration marks as a non-voter is admitted, completes its future without error, and does not install that member as leader; instead the attempt costs an extra election round in which the members' terms advance and leadership ends on a member the caller did not name. Evidence from receipt d436029b08c5425aa5aec577901cb8ba (completed, tests_passed, exit 0; both selected subtests passed). Parsed index 1, the control case where the explicit target is an ordinary voter: target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, future_ok=true, future_ms=2, target_term_after=3 with other_member_term_max_after=3, so the transfer mechanism itself works and advances terms by exactly the election that installs the named target. Parsed index 3, the trigger case where the same cluster demoted the target with DemoteVoter before the transfer: future_ok=true with future_error empty, future_ms=0, target_ever_leader=false, final_leader_is_target=false, target_term_after=4 and other_member_term_max_after=4, while the case event (parsed index 2) records target_demoted=true and transfer_target_role=nonvoter. The two cases differ only in the target's suffrage, so the outcome difference is attributable to eligibility, not to the transfer path, the harness or transport timing. Mechanism from source: leaderLoop resolves an explicit id only through leaderState.replState (raft.go:687-742), which startStopReplication populates for every configured server including non-voters, whereas the automatic path's pickServer skips non-voters outright (raft.go:2186-2206); leadershipTransfer then replicates the target and sends TimeoutNow (raft.go:991-1023), and timeoutNow (raft.go:2232-2237) marks the receiver as a leadership-transfer candidate with no suffrage, term, leader or membership check; electSelf raises the target's term and asks every voter, whose requestVote handler adopts the higher term and steps down before rejecting the non-voter (raft.go:1696-1707). The trigger's term pattern (target and every other member at 4, one step beyond the term the rejected non-voter campaign would have used) matches exactly that path, and the control's single-step advance to 3 matches a successful transfer. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a caller that names a serving but non-voting member gets a completed transfer with no error, no transfer of authority, and a forced election round that raises every voter's term and places leadership elsewhere.

knowledge.assertion: An explicit transfer target is resolved only through leaderState.replState, which includes non-voters, while pickServer skips non-voters.
A voter adopts a higher term and steps down before rejecting a configured non-voter candidate, and timeoutNow forces candidacy without checking suffrage or term.

The claim therefore rests on the admission of an ineligible target and on the observed outcome, not on the future's wording alone.
The control case shows the same mechanism transfers leadership correctly to a voter, so the defect is specific to the eligibility of an explicitly named target, not to leadership transfer in general.

No committed entry was lost, no vote was counted for an ineligible candidate, and no decision-safety property was contradicted in either case; what is contradicted is the completion signal and the authority outcome of the explicit transfer.
limitations: The harness waits 200 ms after DemoteVoter and does not separately assert that the demoted member had received the committed configuration; the voters' rejection and the term pattern are consistent with a non-voter target, but the target's own view of its suffrage at TimeoutNow time was not sampled.

The leaderless interval could not be measured: the sampler produced 43 samples over the 5 s window (about one per 116 ms, not the nominal 10 ms), and no_leader_ms_sampled was 0 in both cases, which is not evidence that leadership was continuously available.

Only one cluster size (four voters) and one demotion position were exercised, and the leader always initiated the transfer to a non-leader member; transfer from a leader that later regains leadership, and clusters whose only non-voter is the sole contactable member, were not tested.

The observation window covered the future's completion and roughly half a second of subsequent leadership sampling; later re-elections that eventually return leadership to the original leader were not tracked, so the persistence of the effect beyond that window is not claimed.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A heartbeat executed on a separate goroutine, as the fast-path contract permits, can persist a term lower than the term the node had already adopted; once the term has regressed the node no longer rejects a stale leader's messages, so it truncates an entry it had already applied at the higher term and applies entries from the stale leader's history. Evidence from receipt cabc782e68fb4c98a4f82a9d4e62e07b (completed, tests_passed, exit 0). Parsed index 1, the term sequence: after_newer_term=4, after_stale_term=3, persisted_term=3, term_decreased=true, and the recorded sequence of persisted current-term writes is [1 1 2 4 3], so the node wrote 4 and then 3. Parsed index 3, the consequence: after the regression the stale term-3 leader's AppendEntries was accepted (stale_request_accepted=true), the log at index 4 became "stale4" while the FSM still holds "new4" there, index 5 was applied from the stale history as "stale5", and applied and commit indexes both reached 5 (applied_entry_replaced=true). Mechanism from source: Transport documents the heartbeat handler as a fast-path, NetworkTransport invokes it from its connection handler, and NewRaft registers r.processHeartbeat (transport.go:58-64, net_transport.go:298-305, api.go:626-632), so appendEntries can run off the main RPC queue; appendEntries tests a.Term above r.getCurrentTerm() and later calls setCurrentTerm(a.Term), which persists and stores the value without re-checking what it read (raft.go:1470-1490, 2164-2172), so an older term decided earlier can land later; the heartbeat request carries no entries, no previous-log term and no commit index (replication.go:388-397), so the regression is the term write itself, and the subsequent acceptance and truncation are performed by the same entry path that trusts the current term (raft.go:1526-1566). Why the comparisons matter: the first asserts Raft's requirement that a server never lowers its persisted term, the second that an entry already applied at a higher term is never replaced; both were contradicted by the same sequence. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a follower with a delayed term write can end at a term below one it already adopted and then accept and apply a stale leader's conflicting entries, leaving its log and FSM describing different histories.

knowledge.assertion: The transport contract permits the registered heartbeat handler to run outside the main RPC queue, and NetworkTransport dispatches heartbeats that way.
appendEntries decides to raise the term, then writes it unconditionally, and a heartbeat's concurrent execution affects only the term and leader.

counterevidence: InmemTransport ignores SetHeartbeatHandler, and the harness therefore invoked r.processHeartbeat directly on a second goroutine rather than exercising a real transport's dispatch, so the transport framing, timeouts and connection lifecycle of NetworkTransport were not part of this observation.

The regression needs the older term write to complete after the newer one; the harness forced that order with a stable-store hook that holds one currentTerm value. Without such a delay the read-then-write pair normally completes in order, and the probe establishes reachability rather than a rate of occurrence.

The stale term-3 and newer term-4 requests were crafted AppendEntries whose leader commit indexes are asserted by the request, not produced by a quorum of live peers; only one real node ran. The claim is therefore about the follower's own duties (term monotonicity and not replacing an applied entry); the divergence from a real committed cluster state is conditional on the term-4 entry having been committed elsewhere.

The applied FSM entry at index 4 was not re-applied because lastApplied already covered that index, so the immediate FSM divergence appeared at index 5; the disagreement at index 4 currently exists only between the log and the FSM, and would surface on a restart replay.
limitations: Single follower, single sequence, one forced interleaving: no repetition, no timing sweep and no concurrent load, so nothing is claimed about how often or how easily this occurs in practice.

The two competing leaders were modelled by crafted requests over the real consumer path; the obsolete leader's partition, its continued heartbeating and the newer leader's quorum were not produced by real nodes.
Only the term and leader writes of the fast-path were exercised; whether other concurrent fast-path effects interact with snapshot installation or configuration updates was not tested.
The fix boundary is unexamined: a compare-and-set term update would close this particular interleaving, but no protective mechanism in the captured code was tested against it.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. knowledge.assertion: The transport contract permits the registered heartbeat handler to run outside the main RPC queue, and NetworkTransport dispatches heartbeats that way.
appendEntries decides to raise the term, then writes it unconditionally, and a heartbeat's concurrent execution affects only the term and leader.

counterevidence: In the retained frequency run the zero-latency case produced no inversion in 200 attempts, so the trigger is latency rather than concurrency alone; a rate below one in two hundred would not have been detected, and this run does not bound the zero-latency rate.

The claim therefore rests on the follower's own duties (term monotonicity and not replacing an applied entry); divergence from a real committed cluster state is conditional on the term-4 entry having been committed elsewhere.

The applied FSM entry at index 4 was not re-applied because lastApplied already covered that index, so the immediate FSM divergence appeared at index 5; the disagreement at index 4 exists between the log and the FSM and would surface on a restart replay.

The probe delivered the heartbeat by calling the registered handler on a separate goroutine rather than through a live NetworkTransport, so framing, connection reuse, timeouts and the response path were not exercised, even though the classified request shape and the direct handler invocation match that transport's source.

The delayed store is a generic hook that sleeps before persisting; no disk-backed store implementation was measured, so nothing is claimed about how often a real stable store's write latency exceeds the interleaving window.

A leadership transfer that explicitly names a member the committed configuration marks as a non-voter is admitted, completes its future without error, and does not install that member as leader; instead the attempt costs an extra election round in which the members' terms advance and leadership ends on a member the caller did not name. Parsed index 1, the control case where the explicit target is an ordinary voter: target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, future_ok=true, future_ms=2, target_term_after=3 with other_member_term_max_after=3, so the transfer mechanism itself works and advances terms by exactly the election that installs the named target. The two cases differ only in the target's suffrage, so the outcome difference is attributable to eligibility, not to the transfer path, the harness or transport timing. Mechanism from source: leaderLoop resolves an explicit id only through leaderState.replState (raft.go:687-742), which startStopReplication populates for every configured server including non-voters, whereas the automatic path's pickServer skips non-voters outright (raft.go:2186-2206); leadershipTransfer then replicates the target and sends TimeoutNow (raft.go:991-1023), and timeoutNow (raft.go:2232-2237) marks the receiver as a leadership-transfer candidate with no suffrage, term, leader or membership check; electSelf raises the target's term and asks every voter, whose requestVote handler adopts the higher term and steps down before rejecting the non-voter (raft.go:1696-1707). The trigger's term pattern (target and every other member at 4, one step beyond the term the rejected non-voter campaign would have used) matches exactly that path, and the control's single-step advance to 3 matches a successful transfer. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a caller that names a serving but non-voting member gets a completed transfer with no error, no transfer of authority, and a forced election round that raises every voter's term and places leadership elsewhere.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A leadership transfer that explicitly names a member the configuration marks as a non-voter is admitted, completes its future without error, and does not install that member as leader; the attempt instead forces an election round in which every member's term advances, leadership lands on a member the caller did not name, and leadership is absent for a measurable interval. Evidence, two receipts of the same experiment lineage. Parsed index 1 of receipt d436029b08c5425aa5aec577901cb8ba and of successor receipt 0726bba116ac415fa38b99b96a88290f, the control where the explicit target is an ordinary voter: target_ever_leader=true, final_leader_is_target=true, future_ok=true, target_term_after=3 with other_member_term_max_after=3, so the mechanism installs the named target with a single term advance. Parsed index 3 of both receipts, the trigger where one non-leader member was demoted with DemoteVoter before the transfer: future_ok=true with an empty future_error, target_ever_leader=false, final_leader_is_target=false, target_term_after=4 and other_member_term_max_after=4, while the case event (parsed index 2) records target_demoted=true and transfer_target_role=nonvoter. A successor run, receipt 4185f1615cf54e4fbd4801044480416d, corrects the earlier measurement: the target's own configuration is read after DemoteVoter returns and polled until it changes (demotion_converged=true, demotion_converge_ms=0), and at the moment the transfer is requested the target itself reports target_role_in_own_config=nonvoter, so the member knew it could not win; it still campaigned (7 candidate samples, 7 leaderless samples, target_term_after=4, target_ever_leader=false, future_ok=true with an empty error) while the voter control at parsed index 1 installed the named target and produced 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples. The trigger produced 8 candidate samples with 8 leaderless samples (about 80 ms with no member reporting Leader) out of 470 samples at roughly 10 ms spacing, against 0 candidate and 0 leaderless samples out of 471 in the control. The two cases differ only in the target's suffrage, so the outcome difference is attributable to eligibility, not to the transfer path, harness or transport timing. Mechanism from source: leaderLoop resolves an explicit id only through leaderState.replState (raft.go:687-742), which startStopReplication populates for every configured server including non-voters, whereas the automatic path's pickServer skips non-voters outright (raft.go:2186-2206); leadershipTransfer replicates the target and sends TimeoutNow (raft.go:991-1023), and timeoutNow (raft.go:2232-2237) marks the receiver as a leadership-transfer candidate with no suffrage, term, leader or membership check; electSelf raises the target's term and asks every voter, whose requestVote handler adopts the higher term and steps down before rejecting the non-voter (raft.go:1696-1707). The trigger's term pattern (target and all other members at 4, one step beyond the rejected round) and its leaderless interval match exactly that path, while the control's single-step advance to 3 matches a successful transfer. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a caller that names a serving but non-voting member receives a completed transfer with no error, no transfer of authority, an extra election round that raises every member's term, and a leaderless interval whose length follows the configured election timeout.

knowledge.assertion: An explicit transfer target is resolved only through leaderState.replState, which includes non-voters, while pickServer skips non-voters.
A voter adopts a higher term and steps down before rejecting a configured non-voter candidate, and timeoutNow forces candidacy without checking suffrage or term.

counterevidence: The documentation's promise is soft rather than a guarantee: it says it is 'very likely' the target wins and that a follower which cannot be promoted 'will fail gracefully' (api.go:1296-1330), and the leaderLoop code deliberately reports nil with the message 'lost leadership during transfer (expected)', which can be read as the future reporting only that leadership was relinquished. The claim therefore rests on the admission of an ineligible target and on the observed outcome, not on the future's wording alone.
The control case shows the same mechanism transfers leadership correctly to a voter, so the defect is specific to the eligibility of an explicitly named target, not to leadership transfer in general.

The measured disruption is small in absolute terms because the cluster ran with inmemConfig timeouts (Heartbeat/Election/Lease 50 ms): 8 samples and about 80 ms without a leader, one extra election round. The interval follows the configured election timeout, so a production configuration of about 1 s would scale it accordingly; the 80 ms figure is not a bound for other settings.

No committed entry was lost, no vote was counted for an ineligible candidate, and no decision-safety property was contradicted in either case; what is contradicted is the completion signal and the authority outcome of the explicit transfer.

The corrected run shows the target's own configuration had already converged to non-voter before the request, so the exercised case is a member that knew it could not win; a demoted member whose own view still lagged (a stale configuration) was not exercised in this receipt, although the earlier runs exercised an unknown mix.
limitations: Both runs exercised one cluster size (four members, three voters after the demotion) and one relationship: a leader transferring to a non-leader member. Transfer initiated while the leader later regains leadership, and clusters whose only non-voter is the sole reachable member, were not tested.

Leaderless counts are sampled every ~10 ms over roughly 4.7 s of the 5 s window (470 samples); a gap shorter than the sample spacing would be missed, so 80 ms is a lower bound for the trigger and the control's zero does not prove uninterrupted leadership.

Only immediate convergence was observed: the demoted member's own view reported the new role within the first poll (0 ms), so no case exercised a target whose configuration still showed it as a voter at request time.
That the voter members had committed the demotion before the transfer is inferred from their rejection and term adoption, not from reading each voter's configuration.

Out of scope: whether an unprivileged or misconfigured peer could send TimeoutNow directly, even though timeoutNow performs no term, leader or membership check (raft.go:2232-2237); that path was not exercised here.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated. With RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft does not complete a legal replay of already-committed log entries once the replay needs more than 128 FSM dispatch batches; the caller never receives the *Raft, so the node has no way to start, serve or shut down. This is a startup progress failure, not a decision-safety failure: no commit, vote or membership decision was observed to be wrong. Evidence. Receipt d61420dbc49a4072937b040aac55a51c (completed, tests_passed, exit 0): parsed index 1, seeded commit-tracking store with 8192 committed entries = exactly 128 batches at MaxAppendEntries=64, returned=true in 5 ms; parsed index 3, the retained state of a real single-node cluster that committed 8300 commands through the leader/commit/apply path and then snapshotted at index 8302 above the staged commit index, replay 0 batches, returned=true in 0 ms; parsed index 5, the same seeded store with 8193 entries = 129 batches, returned=false after 5000 ms with one newly blocked (*Raft).processLogs goroutine and one newly blocked (*Raft).restoreFromCommittedLogs goroutine; parsed index 7, the same real-cluster prefix without a snapshot, staged commit 8300 = 130 batches, returned=false after 5000 ms with the same two newly blocked goroutines. Successor receipt 87aea51bbd8a4b579f138f2c4986343a (completed, tests_passed, exit 0) reproduced all four outcomes (parsed indices 1, 3, 7, 9) and added parsed index 5: the identical 8193-entry store state that hangs at MaxAppendEntries=64, replayed as 9 batches with MaxAppendEntries=1024, returned=true in 2 ms. That comparison holds entry count, log content, staged commit index and snapshot state fixed and varies only the batch size, so the stall is attributable to the number of batches relative to the 128-slot channel rather than to log volume, snapshot handling, store state or the producing cluster; the goroutine match in both hanging cases localizes the block to processLogs invoked from restoreFromCommittedLogs. Mechanism from source: api.go:606 calls restoreFromCommittedLogs before any background goroutine exists; api.go:753 calls processLogs(commitIndex, nil); raft.go:1303-1313 sends each commitTuple batch into fsmMutateCh and selects only on that send and on r.shutdownCh; fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 (api.go:560); its only reader runFSM (fsm.go:241) is started at api.go:637 after NewRaft returns; api.go:1065 is the only closer of shutdownCh and is reachable only through a *Raft. After 128 successful sends the 129th send therefore has no producer and no possible closer, so the block is permanent rather than slow. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a node restarting with the documented RestoreCommittedLogs option and with more than 128*MaxAppendEntries committed entries beyond its last snapshot hangs inside NewRaft indefinitely while reporting no error. The operational restart path was measured separately in receipt f032fc49841048c9877653db9f877b27: a three-voter cluster committed 8400 commands, one follower accumulated them and staged its own commit index at 8400 with last log index 8402, and only that follower was restarted. With a snapshot taken on that follower at 8400 the replay was 0 batches and NewRaft returned in 0 ms (parsed index 1, comparison holds); without the snapshot the same follower needed 132 batches and NewRaft had not returned after 5000 ms (parsed index 3, comparison violated). The boundary therefore reproduces from the follower's own appendEntries-driven commit staging, not only from a feeding leader.

knowledge.assertion: NewRaft calls restoreFromCommittedLogs synchronously and processLogs flushes batches into fsmMutateCh while runFSM starts only after NewRaft returns.
The startup replay can enqueue at most 128 batches, so with DefaultConfig 8193 or more replayed entries beyond the last snapshot have no enabled progress path.

counterevidence: RestoreCommittedLogs is not part of DefaultConfig (config.go:329-341 leaves it false), and with the option disabled restoreFromCommittedLogs returns immediately (api.go:725-727), so default-configured nodes cannot reach the blocked path.

A snapshot at or near the commit index removes the replay entirely: parsed index 3 in both receipts restarted the same 8300-commit real prefix with replay_batches=0 and returned NewRaft immediately, so snapshot cadence bounds exposure to this path.

A larger MaxAppendEntries moves the boundary: parsed index 5 of receipt 87aea51bbd8a4b579f138f2c4986343a completed the very state that hangs at the default batch size, so a deployment that raises MaxAppendEntries enough for 128*MaxAppendEntries to cover its snapshot lag does not encounter the block.

The trigger observations are 5000 ms observation windows, not infinite runs; permanence is claimed from the source-level absence of any consumer before NewRaft returns and from shutdownCh having no closer outside Shutdown on the returned *Raft, not from the timeout alone.
No incorrect commit, applied entry, vote or membership decision was observed in any case; the evidence contradicts only startup progress.
limitations: The boundary is 128*MaxAppendEntries committed entries beyond the last snapshot. Only two batch sizes were exercised (64, boundary 8192, blocked at 8193; 1024, 9 batches, returned); the 128-slot fsmMutateCh capacity itself is not configurable, and no case exercised a replay that lands exactly at 128 batches with a non-default batch size.

The seeded cases supply the commit-tracking store state directly. Three restarts rest on a real prefix: a single-node leader (staged commit 8300, last log 8302, because the leader stages the pre-dispatch commit index) and a three-voter cluster follower in both the snapshot and no-snapshot cases (staged commit 8400, last log 8402).

The with-snapshot control eliminated the replay rather than shortening it, so real-prefix restarts whose replay is between 1 and 128 batches were not exercised; that recovery region is bracketed only by the seeded 9-batch case and inferred from source for the real prefix.

fsm_applied_sampled is one sample at the end of each window and was 0 in every case, including the returning controls where runFSM had not yet applied anything, so it is not used as evidence of completion.

Out of scope here: whether the installSnapshot and restoreUserSnapshot sends to the same channel can block indefinitely on a running node, where runFSM is already active and would provide backpressure rather than a permanent block.

Its cases are named differently and its admissions are its own, so it is not a substitute for the earlier receipts; it is cited because it exercises the same RestoreCommittedLogs replay boundary on the operational restart shape with the same source-level mechanism.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. A heartbeat executed on a goroutine other than the main RPC loop, as the fast-path contract permits, races the node's term update: when the stable-store write it performs takes long enough, the term it decided to persist can land after a higher term already persisted by the main thread, leaving the node below a term it had adopted. Once the term is below the current leader's term, the node stops rejecting an older leader's messages and replaces an entry it had already applied at the higher term with that leader's entry. Evidence. Consequence, receipt cabc782e68fb4c98a4f82a9d4e62e07b: parsed index 1 records after_newer_term=4, after_stale_term=3, persisted_term=3 and the write sequence [1 1 2 4 3] (term_decreased=true); parsed index 3 records the stale term-3 request being accepted (stale_request_accepted=true), the log at index 4 becoming "stale4" while the FSM still holds "new4", index 5 applied from the stale history as "stale5", and both applied and commit indexes at 5 (applied_entry_replaced=true). Frequency, receipt 14a6432138534293b361a796cd32bda8: with no added store latency, 200 concurrent attempts produced inversion_count=0 (parsed index 1, comparison holds), while the same 200 attempts with a uniform 0-2 ms delay added to every current-term write produced inversion_count=90 (parsed index 3, comparison violated). The two cases differ only in that delay, so the inversion is a store-write-latency-sensitive race rather than an artifact of a forced order. Mechanism from source: Transport documents the heartbeat handler as a fast-path (transport.go:58-64); NetworkTransport classifies an AppendEntries as a heartbeat exactly when the term is non-zero, a leader address is present, both previous-log fields are zero, no entries are carried and LeaderCommitIndex is zero - the shape the leader's heartbeat request builds (net_transport.go:660-690, replication.go:388-397) - and for that shape calls the registered handler directly on the connection-handler goroutine, skipping the consumer channel (net_transport.go:718-736), with NewRaft registering r.processHeartbeat (api.go:626-632). appendEntries tests a.Term above r.getCurrentTerm(), then calls setCurrentTerm(a.Term), which writes the stable store and afterwards stores the same value atomically without re-checking (raft.go:1470-1490, 2164-2172); the gap between the store write and the atomic store is where a concurrent higher-term writer can be overtaken. The subsequent acceptance and truncation run on the entry path that trusts the current term (raft.go:1526-1566). Consequence under the exercised conditions: a follower whose stable-store term write is delayed can finish below an already adopted term and then accept and apply a stale leader's conflicting entries, leaving its log and FSM describing different histories. A clean-copy repeat of the same fixed experiment, receipt b89fc1d89b434e8c84a2219073e9a01c, reproduced the pair: parsed index 1 shows inversion_count=0 for the 200 no-delay attempts and parsed index 3 shows inversion_count=97 for the 200 jittered attempts, against 0 and 90 in the first run. The two runs therefore agree that the inversion is absent or rare without added store latency and common with 0-2 ms of it, while the exact count varies between runs.

knowledge.assertion: The transport contract permits the registered heartbeat handler to run outside the main RPC queue, and NetworkTransport dispatches heartbeats that way.
appendEntries decides to raise the term, then writes it unconditionally, and a heartbeat's concurrent execution affects only the term and leader.

counterevidence: In the retained frequency run the zero-latency case produced no inversion in 200 attempts, so the trigger is latency rather than concurrency alone; a rate below one in two hundred would not have been detected, and this run does not bound the zero-latency rate.

The stale term-3 and newer term-4 requests are crafted AppendEntries whose leader commit indexes are asserted by the request, not produced by a quorum of live peers; only one real node ran in either receipt. The claim therefore rests on the follower's own duties (term monotonicity and not replacing an applied entry); divergence from a real committed cluster state is conditional on the term-4 entry having been committed elsewhere.

The applied FSM entry at index 4 was not re-applied because lastApplied already covered that index, so the immediate FSM divergence appeared at index 5; the disagreement at index 4 exists between the log and the FSM and would surface on a restart replay.

The probe delivered the heartbeat by calling the registered handler on a separate goroutine rather than through a live NetworkTransport, so framing, connection reuse, timeouts and the response path were not exercised, even though the classified request shape and the direct handler invocation match that transport's source.

The delayed store is a generic hook that sleeps before persisting; no disk-backed store implementation was measured, so nothing is claimed about how often a real stable store's write latency exceeds the interleaving window.
limitations: Two timing modes, 200 attempts each, repeated twice on one platform: the jittered case produced 90 and then 97 inversions, and the no-delay case produced none in either run. These counts are properties of this harness's delay distribution, not a field rate, and a rate below one in two hundred remains undetected for the no-delay case.

The two competing leaders were modelled by crafted requests over the real consumer path; the obsolete leader's partition, its continued heartbeating and the newer leader's quorum were not produced by real nodes, and repeated attempts reuse one node's log.
Only the term and leader writes of the fast-path were exercised; whether other concurrent fast-path effects interact with snapshot installation or configuration updates was not tested.
The fix boundary is unexamined: a compare-and-set term update would close this interleaving, but no protective mechanism in the captured code was tested against it.

interpretations.rationale: Conclusion: violated, and the scoped defect is asserted. VerifyLeader reports success although the leader can reach fewer voters than the voter quorum it sized, because acknowledgements arriving on non-voter replication streams are counted as support. Evidence from receipt 7a54f3754b0b423aaf1ba6c0365367c0 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0). Parsed index 1, the trigger: five members were bootstrapped, two were demoted to non-voters, and the leader's transport was disconnected in both directions from the two remaining voters, so voters_reachable=1 against quorum_voters=2 while nonvoters_reachable=2; VerifyLeader completed with verify_ok=true and an empty error, and the node was still Leader. Parsed index 3, the control on an identically built cluster with the non-voters also disconnected (nonvoters_reachable=0): the same call completed with verify_ok=false and the error 'leadership lost while committing log', the node by then a Follower. The two cases differ only in whether the non-voters could answer, so the successful verification in the trigger is attributable to non-voter acknowledgements rather than to voter support. Mechanism from source: verifyLeader sets quorumSize with quorumSize(), which counts only voters (raft.go:1087-1100), but registers the verify future on every entry of leaderState.replState (raft.go:966-990), and startStopReplication creates a replication state for every configured server including non-voters (raft.go:583-600); any successful heartbeat or AppendEntries response calls notifyAll(true) (replication.go:100-112), which increments the verify future's vote count (future.go:274-293) and completes it at the voter-sized quorum. The library already uses the correct supporter set one function away: checkLeaderLease iterates the latest configuration and counts only voters (raft.go:1037-1050), so the two paths disagree about who can establish leadership. Consequence under the exercised conditions: a client that calls VerifyLeader to protect a read (api.go:927-931) is told the leader still holds a voter quorum while it can reach none of the other voters, so the guard against serving stale reads after leadership loss does not hold in a cluster that contains non-voters.

knowledge.assertion: VerifyLeader sizes a voter quorum but registers the verification on every replication stream, including non-voters, whose acks increment its vote count.
checkLeaderLease counts only voters, unlike VerifyLeader.

counterevidence: The verification returned before the lease check stepped the leader down, so the false success is bounded by the leader lease interval rather than permanent; in the control that same step-down produced the error the trigger avoided.
VerifyLeader returning nil installed no leader and returned no data; the harm requires a client to rely on it as the guard the documentation describes, and this harness issued no reads.

Non-voter reachability does show the leader is alive and connected, so a deployment that used VerifyLeader only as a liveness probe would not be affected; the code sizes a voter quorum, which makes quorum the stated intent.
The partition was modelled by removing in-memory transport routing in both directions between the leader and the voters, not by dropping packets or crashing members.
limitations: One configuration shape was exercised: three voters and two non-voters, with the leader cut from both other voters. Other suffrage mixes, a single non-voter, or a non-voter whose heartbeat is the only one in flight were not tested.

The exposure window was not measured directly: the harness observed the verification completing immediately after the partition and the leader still in Leader state; how long a false success could persist before the lease check stepped the leader down is bounded by LeaderLeaseTimeout (one second here) but was not sampled.
No client reads were issued, so the end-to-end stale-read consequence is inferred from the documented purpose of VerifyLeader rather than observed.
The demotions completed before the partition, but each member's view of the new configuration was not read back before the transport was cut.
